text: Given a binary tree, determine if it is height-balanced. A height-balanced tree is one where the left and right subtrees of every node differ in height by at most one.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the word I want to grab is every. The rule is not about the root. It has to hold at every single node. Is that right?

I want to sit on that for a second, because it's easy to read past it. A tree can look completely fine at the root and still be unbalanced. The root can have heights three and three, perfectly even, while some node inside has heights zero and two. So a single check at the top is not a weaker version of the answer — it's a different, wrong answer. Also, an empty tree counts as balanced. That's the natural base case. Are there any constraints on the input size?

Let me run through the example: three, nine, twenty, null, null, fifteen, seven. At the root, the left height is one and the right height is two — a gap of one, which is allowed. Node twenty has one and one, and the leaves all have zero and zero. So every node passes, and the answer is true.

Hmm, let me think about this for a sec. A naive approach would be to ignore the every-node part and only check the root. It's one line, and it's wrong — I'll come back with a number on how wrong. This problem reminds me of a post-order height computation, because the height helper is the standard one-plus-max recursion. The only new thing is that I need the height at every node and a yes-or-no answer at every node. There are two ways to put those together. Top-down: at each node, ask for both child heights and check the gap, then recurse into the children. Bottom-up: compute each height once and carry a failed signal up with it. I'll write top-down first because it maps directly onto the definition, and then talk about bottom-up.

Here's the plan. One: a depth helper returns the plain height, zero for empty. Two: an empty tree is balanced. Three: otherwise, the gap at this node must be at most one, and both children must be balanced too, chained with and-and. One thing worth flagging — checking only the root is not a small error. Over every tree shape up to eight nodes, the root-only check is wrong on a hundred sixty-four, and every shape with five nodes or fewer passes by accident. The smallest counterexample needs six nodes: the root sees heights two and three, so it looks fine, but its right child sees zero and two. That's why this bug survives casual tests. There's a trade-off. Top-down reads like the definition but recomputes heights; bottom-up computes each height once but needs a sentinel. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. The empty tree is balanced. Otherwise I take both child depths, and return whether the gap is at most one, and the left subtree is balanced, and the right subtree is balanced. The depth helper is the usual one plus the max of both sides. One thing worth flagging — the and-and here isn't just style. It short-circuits: the moment the gap test fails, both recursive calls are skipped entirely. Hold on to that, because it changes the complexity story in a way people usually get wrong.

Let's dry-run the code with the same tree, expecting true. One row per is-balanced call, with a running count of depth calls. Every node passes, so the answer is true. But look at the last column: twenty-two depth calls for a five-node tree, where the bottom-up version needs eleven. The waste: fifteen and seven are each walked twice — once when the root measures its right side, and again when twenty measures its own sides. In general, a node d levels below the root gets walked d times, once per checked ancestor. Corner cases: an empty tree returns true immediately. A single node has a gap of zero and two null children, so true. The six-node counterexample returns false, failing at the root's right child — exactly what the root-only check misses.

Let me think about complexity here. The usual claim is n squared, with a long chain as the bad case. I want to push back on that, because I measured it. On a chain, the root's gap fails at once, and and-and skips both recursive calls. Chains of two hundred fifty up to two thousand nodes took five hundred up to four thousand depth calls. Doubling the input doubles the work: linear. In general, each node is walked once per checked ancestor, so time is order n times h. A perfect tree gives n log n — nine times the bottom-up count at ten twenty-three nodes, eleven times at four thousand ninety-five. But it can go higher: a comb, a passing spine with stick branches, reaches n to the one point five. Space is order h for the call stack.

Oh, one more thing — the bottom-up version fixes this and is worth writing. One function returns the height, but returns negative one to mean something below me is not balanced. If either child comes back negative one, pass it straight up; if the gap is over one, return negative one; otherwise return one plus the max. That's a single pass, linear time. The sentinel is safe for a specific reason: a real height can never be negative — the smallest honest value is zero, for an empty subtree. If the function could legitimately return a negative, this trick would be unsafe and I'd need a separate flag.

Nicely done. Three things stood out. You caught that balanced is a per-node property, and showed that the smallest counterexample needs six nodes, which is why the bug hides. You corrected the standard n-squared claim with actual call counts, and saw that short-circuiting makes the chain cheap, not expensive. And you explained why negative one is a safe sentinel rather than just using it. Good work.
